title: while True: — The Robot's Heartbeat
description: Real robots don't run once and stop. This is the line of code that keeps ARIA sensing, thinking and acting for as long as she's switched on.

content.value: A Loop With No Planned End

while True: runs its contents over and over, forever, checking nothing but the literal word True — which is, of course, always true. Nested inside it, an if/else can still make the robot's actual behaviour change every single pass, even though the loop itself never stops on its own.

This is the exact shape from the end of Module 9, now in real code. It's also, quite literally, ARIA's heartbeat: sense, decide, act, and immediately start again — never finished, because the real world never stops changing either.

content.title: 🐍 Write the heartbeat
content.hint: Write a real while True: obstacle-avoidance loop. Try tightening the distance threshold and see how it changes the path.

content.value: This simulator gives every run a fixed budget of simulated steps — you can see it happen if you write a while True: loop with no way to reach the goal. That's not a limitation unique to teaching: real embedded systems use the same idea, usually called a watchdog timer, to recover automatically if a program ever gets stuck. "Forever" in a simulator, or on real hardware, is never truly unlimited.

Notice this program has no explicit break or exit anywhere — and that's correct. A real patrol or obstacle-avoiding robot is meant to run until someone switches it off, not until some internal condition says it's done.

Key takeaway: while True: runs forever by design — it's what lets a robot keep reacting to a changing world indefinitely. Real (and simulated) systems still protect against a truly stuck loop with a safety limit underneath.

quiz.question: What does `while True:` check, literally?
options: The literal value True — which never changes, so the loop never ends on its own
Whether the robot is still moving
quiz.explain: It's checking a constant, always-true value. Any actual changing behaviour comes from the code nested inside it, not the loop condition itself.

quiz.question: Why doesn't a well-written obstacle-avoidance program need a break statement?
options: It's meant to run indefinitely, reacting to a changing world, until switched off — not until some condition says 'done'
It always needs one, this is a mistake
quiz.explain: Some robot behaviours are genuinely meant to run forever — a patrol or obstacle-avoider doesn't have a natural finishing point.

quiz.question: What real embedded-systems concept does the simulator's tick budget mirror?
options: A watchdog timer, which recovers a stuck real system automatically
quiz.explain: Real hardware faces the same problem — a genuinely infinite loop needs a safety net, and a watchdog timer is the standard real-world answer.
